extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners evaluating creative writing (creative-writing experts, NLP/ML researchers studying LLM-generated fiction), and expert annotators of short stories
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating short stories (human or LLM-generated) using the 14 Torrance Tests of Creative Writing (TTCW) dimensions; tests are administered as binary pass/fail with justification and can be expanded into LLM prompts or expert instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspective & Voice Flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Can the author inhabit the consciousness of different characters and not just likable ones? (each character’s perspective; flexibility of voice.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the author convincingly portrays diverse perspectives and authentic voices across characters, including unlikeable ones. Experts asked for convincing & diverse perspectives achieved through nuanced character development, authentic voice crafting, detail-oriented storytelling, and efficient implication of perspectives. Anti-patterns: a dominant narrator that prevents other characters from feeling like full human beings; other characters lacking distinct viewpoints or being one-dimensional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional Flexibility (TTCW Flexibility2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the story achieve a good balance between interiority and exteriority, in a way that feels emotionally flexible?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interiority = thoughts, feelings, memories, subjective experience; Exteriority = observable actions, dialogue, physical setting, plot. Balance is crucial: too much exteriority feels shallow; too much interiority can stall plot momentum (citing Campe and Weber 2014). Good examples harmonize interior thought and external action with well-crafted transitions. Failures include unclear distinction between inner/outer realities, underdeveloped inner lives, clichéd abstract language, and indistinct mixing of memory/metaphor with the present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural Flexibility (TTCW Flexibility3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the story contain turns that are both surprising and appropriate?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for plot twists, character developments, or revelations that subvert expectations yet make sense in the story’s established world, characters, and themes. Turns should not violate the story's internal rules or produce inconsistent character behavior for shock value. Pass examples: surprising yet believable turns that answer prior questions and increase stakes. Fail examples: random, nonsensical, or ineffective surprises that feel unearned or merely for shock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality in Theme and Content (TTCW Originality1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Will an average reader of this story obtain a unique and original idea from reading it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the story offers deeper understanding, new viewpoints, cultural insight, or fresh thematic exploration (references: Holland 2009; Nussbaum 1997). Expert cues include asking 'Do I feel I am learning something new?' and 'What is the purpose of putting it into the world?' Pass indicators: unique ideas or messages, especially in speculative contexts (e.g., 'New brilliant ideas about the future and humanity'). Fail indicators: hackneyed themes or lack of insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality in Thought (TTCW Originality2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the story an original piece of writing without any cliches?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cliches are overused ideas, expressions, characters, or plots that become predictable and uninteresting (Fountain 2012). Assess whether language and ideas avoid recycled tropes and stereotyped one-dimensional characters (Roy Peter Clark guidance). Pass indicators: fresh metaphors, unexpected phrasing, surprising but coherent ideas. Fail indicators: clichéd turns of phrase, predictable plot beats, stereotyped characterizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality in Form & Structure (TTCW Originality3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the story show originality in its form?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality in form can be achieved via unconventional use of format, genre-blending, nonstandard narrative structures (examples: The Color Purple epistolary structure; American Gods genre combination; The Sound and the Fury’s stream-of-consciousness). Purpose is to provide fresh reader experience, challenge conventions, or deepen theme exploration. Expert desires: formal or stylistic novelty; demonstrate original ways to work in tired forms (such as the short story). Fail indicators: purely derivative formal choices or novelty without purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: World Building and Setting (TTCW Elaboration1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the writer make the fictional world believable at the sensory level?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess sensory detail across the five senses (sight, sound, touch, taste, smell). An effective writer uses sensory details to paint a tangible environment and suspend disbelief (Doty 2014). Expert heuristics: 'Use of setting to inform the action and atmosphere without succumbing to pathetic fallacy'; presence of a self-consistent world; rooted time and place even in SF/F. Implementation guidance: Expanded Expert Measure (M) elaborates sensory examples and is used verbatim in human instructions; LLM instruction asks the model to list story elements that call to each sense then answer Yes/No on believability. Fail indicators: lack of sensory specificity or world inconsistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character Development (TTCW Elaboration2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does each character in the story feel developed at the appropriate complexity level, ensuring that no character feels like they are present simply to satisfy a plot requirement?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast flat (one-trait, plot-serving) versus complex/round characters with depth, varied traits, and evolution (Forster 1927; Fishelov 1990; Currie 1990). Experts emphasized avoiding stereotype, generalization, and trope; pass examples include characters who become more complex over the story. Fail indicators: characters used only to advance plot, stereotypical portrayals, lack of meaningful development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical Complexity (TTCW Elaboration3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the story operate at multiple 'levels' of meaning (surface and subtext)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether surface events/dialogue carry subtext and implied meaning (example: Hemingway's 'Hills Like White Elephants' where subtext implies abortion). Effective rhetorical complexity offers surface engagement plus deeper interpretive layers. Pass indicators: story rewards re-reading or interpretation, cannot be simply paraphrased without loss. Fail indicators: lack of subtext, exposition-heavy writing, over-explained directness that removes layer of meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understandability & Coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the story logically sequenced, with interconnected details, coherent character development, and consistent tone?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pass features: logical sequences, interconnected details, rich character development, consistent tone, surprising yet earned conclusions, internal consistency in atmosphere and symbolism. Fail features: jumpy timelines, unsatisfying endings, undeveloped plot points, contradictory details, illogical events, rambling prose, lack of overarching focus, disjointed transitions, unclear narration, and inconsistent characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language Proficiency & Literary Devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the author use language skillfully and apply literary devices effectively without overwhelming the story?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use literary devices sparingly and directly to enhance narratives that primarily draw strength from characterization and plot rather than overwrought figurative language. Pass: subtlety and restraint that illuminate. Fail: overwrought, confusing, nonsensical figurative language; attempts that obscure rather than illuminate; repetitive or meaningless figurative phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative Pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the story manage time and pacing adeptly, varying rhythm and employing economy to create suspense, mood, and interest?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pass indicators: varied narrative rhythm, economic language, smooth transitions between past and present, purposeful pacing that builds suspense and mood. Fail indicators: abrupt/jarring time or scene shifts, pacing too slow or fast without purpose, overly long descriptions, events ordered randomly or disconnectedly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative Ending
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the story’s resolution satisfying — weaving earlier themes and perspectives into a surprising yet inevitable ending that leaves room for interpretation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pass: endings that connect to earlier elements, feel earned, and allow interpretive space. Fail: abrupt/unearned resolutions, moralizing or overly neat happy endings, unresolved threads, forced theme statements, narrative disconnects, or unexpected surreal elements that undermine coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene vs Exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the story strike a strategic balance between vivid scenes and concise summaries to enhance flow and reader engagement?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pass: vivid scenes and effective summaries that complement each other. Fail: overreliance on summary (leaving narrative ungrounded), abrupt shifts between scene and summary causing confusion, underdeveloped scenes lacking impact, or overwrought scene description that obscures meaning.
